opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing is to be very clear about the problem you're solving, independent of the technology. With hype it's easy to start from "we have this amazing model, what can we do with it?" Usually the more durable companies start from "here's a painful problem people have today, and AI finally makes a much better solution possible."

Second, be realistic about where the technology is. These models are incredibly capable, but they're not perfectly reliable. They hallucinate, they can be inconsistent, and their quality varies a lot across tasks. So pick applications where you can tolerate some errors, or where you can build mechanisms around the model to catch and correct them: verification, human in the loop, retrieval, evaluation pipelines. A lot of the real engineering work and a lot of the moat is in that system around the model, not in the model alone.

Third, assume the underlying models will keep getting better and cheaper, quickly. If your whole value proposition is a thin wrapper that compensates for a weakness of today's model, the next release may wipe it out. Ask yourself: if the model becomes ten times better and ten times cheaper next year, does my business get stronger or does it disappear? You want the answer to be "stronger." That usually means owning the workflow, the data, the integration into how customers actually work, and the feedback loop that lets you improve over time.

And finally, from my experience with Databricks and Anyscale: focus matters a lot early on. There's a temptation in a hype cycle to chase every opportunity because everything looks possible. But you win by being dramatically better for a specific set of users, earning their trust, and then expanding from there. The hype will come and go; what lasts is whether you actually deliver value people are willing to pay for.

r001.rationale: The response recommends starting from customer problems and building reliable systems, but it does not explicitly recommend prioritizing production over demonstrations.

r002.rationale: It warns that hype can tempt founders to chase many opportunities and notes current model limitations, but does not clearly say hype leads founders to overestimate which problems they can currently solve.

r003.rationale: The response advocates solving a painful problem and focusing on specific users, but does not state that solving a smaller version of the intended problem can still deliver substantial customer value.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll write the guest turn directly, speaking as Ion Stoica.

Guest: I think the first thing is to not let the hype dictate what you build. The hype is about the models, but the models are becoming more and more of a commodity. Every few months there is a new one that is better, cheaper, or open. If your entire value is a thin wrapper around someone else's model, you are in a very fragile position, because whatever you did, the next model release can do out of the box.

So the question I would ask a founder is: what is the problem you are solving, and who is the user? Start from a real workflow where people today spend a lot of time or money, and where even an imperfect answer is valuable. Then figure out what the model is actually good at, and build the system around it. In practice, the model is a small part of that system. There is the data, the retrieval, the tooling, the evaluation, the guardrails, the integration into how the user actually works. That is where most of the engineering goes, and honestly that is where most of the defensibility comes from.

The second thing is evaluation. This is something I keep repeating. With traditional software you can write a test and it passes or it fails. With these models, the behavior is probabilistic, and it changes when you change the prompt, the model, the data. If you do not have a way to measure quality on your own task, you are flying blind. You will not know whether a new model is actually better for you, or whether you just broke something. So building your own evaluation, on your own data, early, is one of the highest-leverage things you can do.

And the third thing, I would say, is to be pragmatic about cost and latency. In the demo nobody cares. In production, if every request costs you a dollar and takes thirty seconds, you do not have a business. So think about where you can use smaller models, caching, routing, and when you really need the frontier model. These are the kinds of systems problems we have been working on with things like vLLM, and they matter a lot more than people expect once you have real users.

So, in short: find a real problem, treat the model as a replaceable component, invest in evaluation, and think about the economics from day one. The hype will come and go. The applications that survive are the ones that are actually useful to someone.

r001.rationale: It urges founders to build for real workflows and production users, and contrasts production costs and latency with demos.

r002.rationale: It cautions against letting hype dictate what to build, but does not say hype leads founders to overestimate which problems current AI can solve.

r003.rationale: It says an imperfect answer can be valuable, but does not state that solving a smaller version of the intended problem can still deliver substantial customer value.

astra-6.text:
I think you should start with the problem you want to solve, rather than with the technology. Who is the customer? What are they doing today, and how can you make that substantially better? AI may allow you to do something that was not possible before, but you still have to demonstrate value.

Then get something in front of users quickly. It is easy to build an impressive demo. The harder question is whether it works reliably on the problems customers actually have, at a cost they are willing to pay. That is what you need to learn early.

And assume the technology will keep changing. You want to benefit from better models, so be careful about building a company around a limitation that the next model might remove. Focus on understanding the customer and delivering something they keep using.

r001.rationale: It contrasts an impressive demo with whether the application works reliably on customers’ actual problems and urges learning that early.

r002.rationale: It says AI may enable previously impossible things and advises proving value, but does not warn that hype leads founders to overestimate what problems they can currently solve.

r003.rationale: It recommends delivering something customers keep using, but does not state that solving a smaller version of the intended problem can still provide substantial value.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to start with the problem you are solving for the customer. AI gives you a new set of tools, but the customer still cares about whether your product saves time, reduces cost, or lets them do something they could not do before.

So build something small, put it in front of users, and measure the value. With AI, a demo can be very impressive, but you need to understand how reliably it works on real customer tasks and how much it costs to deliver that result.

And expect the technology to change. Models will improve, so you should keep asking: if the model becomes much better tomorrow, does that make my application more useful? Ideally, your advantage comes from understanding the customer's workflow and delivering a complete solution.

r001.rationale: It contrasts an impressive demo with reliability and cost on real customer tasks, and recommends putting a small product in front of users to measure value.

r002.rationale: It discusses AI hype and changing models but does not warn that hype may lead founders to overestimate what problems they can currently solve.

r003.rationale: It recommends building something small, but does not say that a smaller version of the intended problem can still deliver substantial customer value.
